paraphrase: Taking up this impure image (the body), the awakening mind transforms it into the priceless image of a Victor's jewel; so hold firmly to this quicksilver-elixir called the awakening mind.

paraphrase: In brief, the awakening mind is to be known as twofold: the mind aspiring to awakening and the mind proceeding to awakening; as the difference between one who wishes to go and one who is going is understood, so the wise should understand the difference between these two in order.

paraphrase: As long as space remains and as long as the world remains, so long may I remain, destroying the sufferings of the world. Whatever suffering the world has, may it all ripen in me; and may the world be happy through all the virtues of the bodhisattvas.

original.text: ākāśasya sthitir yāvad yāvac ca jagataḥ sthitiḥ | tāvanmama sthitir bhūyāj jagadduḥkhāni nighnataḥ || yat kiṃcij jagato duḥkhaṃ tat sarvaṃ mayi pacyatām | bodhisattvaśubhaiḥ sarvairjagat sukhitamastu ca

paraphrase: Whatever evil I, like a beast, have done or caused to be done in beginningless saṃsāra or in this very life — (I confess it).

paraphrase: Today I go for refuge to the Protectors of the world, of great power, striving to guard the world and removing all fear; and I go for refuge with all my heart to the Dharma they realized, which destroys the fear of saṃsāra, and likewise to the assembly of bodhisattvas.

original.text: adyaiva śaraṇaṃ yāmi jagannāthān mahābalān | jagadrakṣārtham udyuktān sarvatrāsaharāñjinān || taiścāpyadhigataṃ dharmaṃ saṃsārabhayanāśanam | śaraṇaṃ yāmi bhāvena bodhisattvagaṇaṃ tathā

paraphrase: Leaving this world of the living and my relatives and acquaintances, I shall go somewhere alone; what use to me are all things dear and not dear?

paraphrase: Whatever evil I, foolish and deluded, have accumulated — what is blameworthy by nature and what is blameworthy by precept — all this I confess, standing before the Protectors with joined palms, afraid of suffering, bowing again and again. original.text: mayā bālena mūḍhena yatkiṃcitpāpamācitam | prakṛtyā yac ca sāvadyaṃ prajñaptyāvadyameva ca || tatsarvaṃ deśayāmyeṣa nāthānāmagrataḥ sthitaḥ | kṛtāñjalirduḥkhabhītaḥ praṇipatya punaḥ punaḥ || atyayamatyayatvena pratigṛhṇantu nāyakāḥ | na bhadrakamidaṃ nāthā na kartavyaṃ punarmayā

paraphrase: Just as the Sugatas of old took up the awakening mind and established themselves step by step in the bodhisattva trainings, so I too generate the awakening mind for the good of the world, and so I will train in those trainings in due order.

paraphrase: My enemies, craving, hatred and the rest, have no hands or feet, are neither brave nor wise; how have they made me their slave?

paraphrase: It is said that one who has thought of giving even a trifling thing and does not give it becomes a hungry ghost; how much worse, then, if having loudly invited the whole world to supreme happiness I deceive it — what destiny will be mine?

original.text: manasā cintayitvāpi yo na dadyātpunarnaraḥ | sa preto bhavatītyuktam alpamātre'pi vastuni || kimutānuttaraṃ saukhyam uccair uddhuṣya bhāvataḥ | jagatsarvaṃ visaṃvādya kā gatirme bhaviṣyati

paraphrase: One who wishes to guard the training must guard the mind with effort; the training cannot be guarded without guarding the restless mind. Untamed rutting elephants do not cause such harm as the unleashed elephant of mind causes in the Avīci hell; if the elephant of mind is bound on all sides with the rope of mindfulness, all fear vanishes and all good comes.

original.text: śikṣāṃ rakṣitukāmena cittaṃ rakṣyaṃ prayatnataḥ | na śikṣā rakṣituṃ śakyā calaṃ cittamarakṣatā || adāntā mattamātaṃgā na kurvantīha tāṃ vyathām | karoti yāmavīcyādau muktaścittamataṃgajaḥ || baddhaś cec cittamātaṃgaḥ smṛtirajjvā samantataḥ | bhayamastaṃ gataṃ sarvaṃ kṛtsnaṃ kalyāṇamāgatam

paraphrase: In brief, this alone is the mark of introspection: to examine again and again the state of body and mind.

paraphrase: One should not harm the body, which serves the true Dharma, for a lesser purpose; so one can quickly fulfil the hopes of beings. Therefore one should not give up one's life while the intention of compassion is impure; when the intention is equal (for self and others), it may be given up — so nothing is lost.

original.text: saddharmasevakaṃ kāyamitarārthe na pīḍayet | evameva hi sattvānām āśāmāśu prapūrayet || tyajen na jīvitaṃ tasmādaśuddhe karuṇāśaye | tulyāśaye tu tattyājyamitthaṃ na parihīyate

paraphrase: Whatever good conduct — giving, worship of the Sugatas — has been done over thousands of aeons, anger destroys it. There is no evil equal to hatred and no austerity equal to patience; therefore one should cultivate patience with effort in various ways.

original.text: sarvam etatsucaritaṃ dānaṃ sugatapūjanam | kṛtaṃ kalpasahasrairyatpratighaḥ pratihanti tat || na ca dveṣasamaṃ pāpaṃ na ca kṣāntisamaṃ tapaḥ | tasmāt kṣāntiṃ prayatnena bhāvayedvividhairnayaiḥ

paraphrase: If there is a remedy, what is the use of being unhappy about it? And if there is no remedy, what is the use of being unhappy about it?

paraphrase: What is vigour? Delight in the good. Its opposite is called laziness, attachment to what is base, despondency and self-contempt.

paraphrase: Having increased vigour, one should settle the mind in concentration, for a person with a distracted mind stands between the fangs of the afflictions; by solitude of body and mind distraction does not occur, so one should renounce the world and give up discursive thoughts. Knowing that one endowed with insight together with calm destroys the afflictions, one should first seek calm, and it comes through delight free of worldly attachment.
notes: Original of 8.1, 8.2 and 8.4 read in the DCS text (8.3 not checked).

paraphrase: Whoever wishes quickly to protect both himself and others should practise the supreme secret: the exchange of self and other.

original.text: ātmānaṃ ca parāṃścaiva yaḥ śīghraṃ trātumicchati | sa caretparamaṃ guhyaṃ parātmaparivartanam

paraphrase: All who are unhappy in the world are so through desiring their own happiness; all who are happy are so through desiring others' happiness. What need of more words? See the difference between the fool who works for himself and the sage who works for others. Without exchanging one's own happiness for others' suffering, buddhahood is not achieved, and even in saṃsāra there is no happiness.

original.text: ye kecid duḥkhitā loke sarve te svasukhecchayā | ye kecit sukhitā loke sarve te 'nyasukhecchayā || bahunā vā kimuktena dṛśyatāmidamantaram | svārthārthinaśca bālasya muneścānyārthakāriṇaḥ || na nāma sādhyaṃ buddhatvaṃ saṃsāre'pi kutaḥ sukham | svasukhasyānyaduḥkhena parivartamakurvataḥ

paraphrase: Whatever calamities, sufferings and fears there are in the world all come from grasping at a self; what use is this grasping to me? Without giving up the self one cannot give up suffering, as one cannot avoid burning without giving up fire. Therefore, to calm my own suffering and the suffering of others, I give myself to others and accept others as myself.
notes: Originals of 8.134–136 read in DCS (8.134 has the typo 'koke' for 'loke').

paraphrase: At first one should earnestly cultivate the equality of self and others: all, equal in suffering and happiness, are to be protected by me as myself. As the body, though divided into many parts such as hands, is to be protected as one, so this whole world, divided but undivided in its nature of suffering and happiness, (is to be protected as one).

original.text: parātmasamatāmādau bhāvayedevamādarāt | samaduḥkhasukhāḥ sarve pālanīyā mayātmavat || hastādibhedena bahuprakāraḥ kāyo yathaikaḥ paripālanīyaḥ | tathā jagadbhinnamabhinnaduḥkhasukhātmakaṃ sarvamidaṃ tathaiva

paraphrase: When happiness is equally dear to me and to others, what is special about myself that I strive for happiness for myself alone? When fear and suffering are equally unwelcome to me and to others, what is special about myself that I protect myself and not the other?

paraphrase: The Sage taught this whole set of practices for the sake of wisdom; therefore one who wishes to end suffering should generate wisdom.

original.edition: Bodhicaryāvatāra, DCS corpus (sources_raw/dcs, BoCA), verses reconstructed from the sentence halves

paraphrase: 'Īśvara is the cause of the world' — then tell me who Īśvara is. If the elements, so be it — why labour over a mere name? But they are many, impermanent, inert, not divine, trodden on and impure; the earth and the rest are not Īśvara. If the Lord creates without wishing, he depends on another; if wishing, he depends on his wish — so where is his lordship in creating?
notes: Originals of 9.119, 9.120 and 9.126 read in DCS.

paraphrase: (Against mind-only:) If mind itself were the illusion, what would see what? The Protector of the world said that mind does not see mind.
notes: Summary of the exchange in 9.15–17 (originals read in DCS); speaker attributions follow Prajñākaramati.

paraphrase: Thus there is no contradiction, and no entity at all exists; therefore this whole world is unborn and unceasing. The destinies are like dreams and, under analysis, like a plantain tree; between those who have reached nirvāṇa and those who have not there is no difference in reality.

original.text: evaṃ ca na virodho'sti na ca bhāvo'sti sarvadā | ajātam aniruddhaṃ ca tasmātsarvamidaṃ jagat || svapnopamāstu gatayo vicāre kadalīsamāḥ | nirvṛtānirvṛtānāṃ ca viśeṣo nāsti vastutaḥ

paraphrase: Conventional and ultimate — these are held to be the two truths; reality is not the domain of the intellect; the intellect is said to be conventional.

paraphrase: Here the world is seen as twofold, the yogin and the ordinary person; the ordinary world is refuted by the world of yogins.

paraphrase: By habituation to emptiness the habit of taking things as real is removed; by habituation to 'nothing exists' that too is later abandoned. When no thing is found which is conceived as not existing, how can non-existence, without a basis, stand before the mind? When neither being nor non-being remains before the mind, then, since there is no other way, it is pacified without an object.

original.text: śūnyatāvāsanādhānāddhīyate bhāvavāsanā | kiṃcin nāstīti cābhyāsāt sāpi paścāt prahīyate || yadā na labhyate bhāvo yo nāstīti prakalpyate | tadā nirāśrayo'bhāvaḥ kathaṃ tiṣṭhenmateḥ puraḥ || yadā na bhāvo nābhāvo mateḥ saṃtiṣṭhate puraḥ | tadānyagatyabhāvena nirālambā praśāmyate

paraphrase: (Objection:) liberation comes from seeing the (four) truths; what need of seeing emptiness? (Reply:) because scripture says there is no awakening without this path. If you say the Mahāyāna is unestablished, how is your own scripture established? Whatever reason makes you trust it, apply that to the Mahāyāna too.

So no fault applies to the side of emptiness, and emptiness should be cultivated without doubt; emptiness is the antidote to the darkness of the obscurations of afflictions and of the knowable — how could one who wishes quickly for omniscience not cultivate it?

original.text: tadevaṃ śūnyatāpakṣe dūṣaṇaṃ nopapadyate | tasmān nirvicikitsena bhāvanīyaiva śūnyatā || kleśajñeyāvṛtitamaḥ pratipakṣo hi śūnyatā | śīghraṃ sarvajñatākāmo na bhāvayati tāṃ katham

paraphrase: Let fear arise from what produces suffering; emptiness calms suffering, so why should fear arise from it? If there were any 'I', let there be fear from anything; but if 'I' is nothing at all, whose will the fear be?

paraphrase: The one who has the cause is seen to be joined with the result — this is not possible; the agent and the enjoyer are taught with reference to the unity of a continuum.
